The rise of two such figures into the command posts of Nepal’s economic machinery is therefore a reminder that the country has been producing technical minds for decades, even when the state has not always known how to use them.

The importance of this pairing lies in its potential to reduce an old institutional quarrel. When the finance minister speaks of reforming outdated laws, digitising revenue, reducing discretionary power, and improving the quality of public spending, the central bank should not be treated as an opponent. When the governor worries about liquidity, inflation, foreign exchange reserves, banking discipline, or international financial-compliance pressures, the finance ministry should not see those concerns as mere obstruction. A serious state needs both ambition and restraint. It needs fiscal energy joined to monetary credibility.

This is the architecture of fiscal sovereignty. Sovereignty is not proved only by slogans, flags, or defiance of outsiders. It is proved when a country can finance its priorities, regulate its credit system, protect its currency, raise revenue fairly, and create conditions for productive investment. That requires the Ministry of Finance and the central bank to speak not just politely, but intelligently and consistently.

India’s 1991 economic reforms were not the work of one heroic official acting alone. They emerged from a rare alignment of political authority and technical competence: Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao gave space to Manmohan Singh at Finance, while figures such as P. Chidambaram in Commerce and Montek Singh Ahluwalia in the senior policy bureaucracy helped translate reformist diagnosis into administrative action. The context was very different from Nepal’s, and the comparison should not be stretched too far. But one lesson travels well: Structural reform requires a small group of people who share a diagnosis and trust one another enough to act.

Nepal’s economic-policy corridor, from Singha Durbar through Maitighar to Thapathali, has not lacked seriously trained figures. During the state-building decades after 1951, institutional pioneers and trained economists such as Himalaya SJB Rana, Bhekh Bahadur Thapa and Yadav Prasad Pant helped bring academic preparation and economic discipline into fiscal administration. In democratic politics too, leaders such as Bharat Mohan Adhikari, Ram Sharan Mahat, Prakash Chandra Lohani, Prakash Sharan Mahat, Yuba Raj Khatiwada and Minendra Rijal show that learning and policy seriousness have never been absent from economic public life.

This is where the idea of ‘Nationalist Technocrat’ becomes useful. A nationalist technocrat uses technical competence to enlarge the state’s capacity and protect the public interest. The nationalist part commits to national resilience. The technocratic part maintains discipline, evidence and institutional design.

Nepal’s economy remains too dependent on remittances, import taxation, real-estate cycles, and consumption rather than production. Young people continue to leave because the domestic economy cannot absorb their ambition. Public revenue is squeezed, but citizens still expect roads, schools, hospitals, jobs and basic services. The private sector asks for policy stability, while the state often changes rules faster than investors can make plans.

This moment should therefore be used for durable reform. Nepal needs a simpler and more credible tax system, cleaner revenue administration, stronger protection against arbitrary ministerial discretion, better public investment selection, and a financial system that rewards production rather than speculation. It also needs laws and institutions that can survive changes in coalition politics.

No pair of officials can transform an economy by themselves. Democratic consent, parliamentary debate, provincial coordination, and public trust all matter. But when the finance ministry and the central bank are led by people who can understand each other’s language, the country receives a rare chance to move from reaction to design.

Nepal’s future will not be secured by personality alone, even by talented personalities. It will be secured when the state learns how to place serious expertise inside public institutions, pair authority with accountability, and make institutions work in concert. Singha Durbar and Thapathali are already close on the map; the real task is to make them close in purpose.

articles.title: Time to introduce charter schools in Nepal?
articles.summary:
Nepal’s public education system has been in shambles for a long time due to political instability and poor governance, as documented in a collection of research papers published by Martin Chautari, School Education in Nepal (2021). Recent directives issued by the Minister of Education and Sports, Sasmit Pokharel, are attempts to alter course. The current government might indeed be equipped to make sweeping changes due to its historic mandate. Following one of Minister Pokharel’s directives, the Curriculum Development Centre is in the process of revising the school-level National Curriculum Framework (NCF) under a task force led by the Dean of Kathmandu University’s School of Education. “The goal is not cosmetic change but systemic transformation…and the new NCF must be relevant, responsive and rigorous,” he implored at the mid-July orientation session.

Radical restructuring?

Despite good intentions, the NCF revision may not translate to actual change on the ground. Several studies, such as the report by the U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre—Reforming Nepal’s education system for greater integrity and improved outcomes—have pointed out glaring disconnects between policies and practice in Nepal’s education sector over the decades due to a culture of corruption, fragile monitoring systems, improper teacher management, and a general lack of trust. It might be time to introduce innovative models of school structure and governance, such as charter schools, which function on the basis of a contract between the government and a committee of stakeholders.

Funded by the government but operating with a degree of autonomy, the first charter school started in Minnesota in the United States in 1991. Since then, it has spread across the country, with each state having their own laws governing the establishment, regulation and functioning of charter schools. Similar public-private models have since been running in other developed countries like the UK, Canada and Sweden. Japan, Pakistan and Qatar also have similar models. An article published in 2016 by the National Association of Charter School Authorizers described how New Delhi was also considering ‘government partnership’ schools that would bring in private operators to run public schools.

Attempts at decentralising education

During the first half of the 20th century, most public schools in Nepal were founded and managed by local communities, and were called by different names based on differing principles and goals: English, Bhasha, Basic, Sanskrit and so on. In 1957, massive protests erupted, especially in Tarai, against the government’s directive to use Nepali as a medium of instruction in all schools. Later, the Panchayat government (1960–1990) took control of the education system, mandating “a uniform education system in the country with a single language of instruction”. Nationalising and centralising the education system in a diverse, multicultural society was like trying to put a square peg in a round hole.

After the dawn of democracy and neoliberalism in the 1990s, the private sector proliferated and public schools deteriorated. The state began a process of decentralisation in the early 2000s, but the ongoing People’s War hampered these efforts. Federalism and a demand for decentralisation were a response to the centralised bureaucracy detached and disconnected from most of the country. Although the current Constitution of Nepal explicitly grants local governments authority to manage all aspects of school education, this has been a point of contention, with teachers’ unions staging protests, wanting to be part of the cadre of the central government.

From chaos comes order

A paper published by Kuber Prasad Bhetwal in 2022, Effectiveness of Local Curriculum Implementation in Nepal, has a list of findings and suggestions from his field study in Sankhuwasaba’s primary schools. Most interviewed teachers supported teaching local curricula that include local issues. Charter schools could similarly be founded with goals and visions that suit local culture, language and needs. But the paper also identifies that building new curricula and systems is hampered by a lack of human resources. Sankhuwasaba’s district administrative personnel had minimal experience with local curriculum development and implementation.

Given Nepal’s multilingual, multiethnic reality, provincial and local governments are best positioned to deliver education. They should be supported to design unique charter schools and hire and train experts who are more responsive to and knowledgeable about local issues. Perhaps a radical systemic restructuring will be a worthy experiment, although we have to be wary of commercial interests, especially in the delivery of public services. There is already widespread discontent regarding a lack of proper regulation of profit-seeking private schools. But I’m simply offering an option out of the quagmire that has been Nepal’s public education system.

We must consider alternatives suitable for a diverse populace. Charter schools won’t be perfect, but a massive overhaul will create opportunities to tap into young talents and mobilise them across the country—similar to how Teach for Nepal has been functioning. Since we already have three tiers of government, and the Federal Education Act has still not been passed, this might be a moment to truly imagine a new system that could work with the local and provincial governments to deliver educational services effectively and efficiently. It will undoubtedly be extremely challenging to imagine and implement large-scale changes. But if the government is indeed serious about improving public services and creating a long-lasting impact, it should take bold, radical steps and make arrangements accordingly.

articles.title: It takes a global village
articles.summary:
Nepal has roughly $53 billion sitting in bank deposits. Around $14 billion enters the country each year through remittances. Its technology sector is now estimated to export more than $1 billion in services. Yet, promising Nepali enterprises still struggle to find the capital, capabilities and markets they need to scale.

That paradox has become harder to ignore as traditional development finance contracts. Official development assistance fell by 23 percent globally in 2025, its largest annual contraction on record, with a further decline projected in 2026. Nepal is simultaneously preparing to graduate from the Least Developed Country status, even as AI rapidly reshapes economies, organisations and the capabilities they need.

Perhaps, then, the question is not only what Nepal lacks. It is why so much of what we already have remains difficult to connect, mobilise and scale.

For me, that question became personal over the past year. After nearly two decades in international development, including more than a decade at USAID, I found myself reconsidering some of the assumptions that had shaped my own career: what was worth carrying forward, what needed to change, and where institutions like ours could add distinctive value.

Over the year, our team worked across all seven provinces and encountered the same paradox.

Entrepreneurs were looking for investors; investors for investment-ready enterprises. Universities were producing graduates; employers were struggling to find the capabilities they needed. Researchers were generating useful evidence, but practitioners often struggled to find, translate or apply it. Development organisations were piloting solutions; businesses with the technology, networks or commercial incentives to help them scale were often not in the same room. More than a shortage of effort, ideas or resources, the constraint was the pathways between them.

We talk a great deal about physical infrastructure in Nepal, and rightly so. But economies also depend on intangible infrastructure: trust, relationships, shared knowledge, credible intermediaries and networks that allow capital, talent and ideas to find one another—and promising solutions to scale.

For instance, $7,200 from FCDO’s Nepal in Business-Growth Advisors programme funded an investment-readiness initiative that we delivered for Nepali technology companies. One participant, Raindrop, went on to secure a strategic partner who brings deep expertise as well as investment of approximately $131,000—more than 18 times that initial investment.

Consider the wider capital landscape: roughly $53 billion in bank deposits, $39 billion in lending, and around $14 billion in annual remittances, compared with a federal capital budget of about $14 billion and roughly $400 million in foreign grants. Capital and opportunity exist, but the structures, information, incentives and trust that allow them to meet often do not.

When grants can no longer be assumed—or sustained at familiar scale—what other assets do organisations have to work with? Quite a lot: community trust; deep local networks; institutional knowledge of what localisation, inclusion and equity require in practice; relationships across sectors; data; convening power; and implementation capability.

These assets have economic value too. Private capital cannot replace public or philanthropic resources where markets cannot or will not go. But development resources should be judged not only by what they finance, but by what they unlock: the risk absorbed, institution strengthened, evidence generated, relationship brokered, capability left behind or capital subsequently moved.

So the questions should not only be ‘what did we spend?’, ‘what did we deliver?’, and ‘how many people did we reach?’ But also ‘what did we unlock?’, ‘what became possible because we were there?’, and ‘what keeps moving when we’re gone?’

The same shift, from looking for what is missing to recognising what already exists, raises a larger question: Could this disruption also change how countries like Nepal are seen globally?

For decades, countries like ours have occupied a familiar position in the global development architecture—recipients of money, expertise, technology and ideas.

But Nepal is also a source of them. Companies like Programiz, Veel and SecurityPal AI are building from Nepal for global markets, and industry estimates put Nepal’s IT services exports at over $1 billion. Pukar Hamal, founder of SecurityPal AI, describes this potential as ‘Silicon Peaks’—a vision of Nepal not simply as a source of global talent, but as a place where technology, companies and ideas can be built for the world.

Add to that a diaspora carrying expertise, relationships and capital across borders, communities and institutions with knowledge outsiders do not possess, and a generation of young Nepalis whose professional and technological horizons are increasingly global.

The next chapter of Nepal’s growth must be as much about recognising, connecting, investing in and amplifying existing strengths as filling gaps.

Perhaps the opportunity, then, is not simply to attract more resources into Nepal, but to build pathways that allow what Nepal already has to reach further—to opportunities at home, capital and markets abroad, and problems elsewhere that Nepali talent and enterprise can help solve.

Nepal’s greatest untapped potential may lie not in any single institution, sector or source of capital, but in what becomes possible when their strengths come together.

We already have many of the ingredients. The opportunity is to make it easier for these assets to find and reinforce one another, at home and across borders.

Nepal does not sit outside that global village waiting to be helped. We are already part of it, with locally brewed talent, knowledge systems, enterprise and solutions to contribute. But a village is not simply a network to draw from. It requires reciprocity: contributing as well as receiving, sharing what we know and have, and investing in one another's success.

A village is not made strong by its individual houses, but by the roads between them, and people choosing to use them. Those are the roads I want us to continue strengthening: between entrepreneurs and investors, universities and businesses, communities and markets, public purpose and private initiative, Nepal and the world.

Locally led, globally connected. Because when the right ideas find the right support, what begins here can go much further.

articles.title: No decision yet on Bangladesh PM’s visit to India, Dhaka says
articles.summary:
Bangladesh has not made a decision yet on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s ​visit to India, his press secretary said on Friday, ‌after Indian media reported that Rahman would be visiting New Delhi from August 23-25.

The South Asian neighbours have been in talks for weeks regarding Rahman’s first ​trip to New Delhi since taking office in February, as ​they work to repair ties strained by the 2024 ouster of Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

Hasina fled to India ​after student-led protests ended her long rule and has lived there in ​exile. Dhaka has repeatedly asked New Delhi to extradite her. India has said that it is examining the request.

“No decision has yet been made on the ​visit,” Rahman’s Press Secretary A A M Saleh told Reuters, adding ​that Dhaka was waiting for India’s response on the extradition of Hasina and “other fugitive ‌criminals”.

The Indian foreign ministry did not have any comments to make on the visit, Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters at a regular media briefing.

Rahman’s six-month-old government has sought to maintain good relations with India since ​coming to power, ​but signalled last ⁠week that a more favourable diplomatic environment was needed for the trip, days after Hasina addressed journalists in ​a move condemned by Dhaka.

Forced to flee Bangladesh ​following violent protests against her government, Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia in November for ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising.

She has denied the ​charges, dismissing them as politically motivated, and ​told reporters that she would return to her country in December.

articles.title: Europe’s hottest town says climate change is reshaping daily life
articles.summary:
Five years after Floridia registered Europe’s highest-ever temperature, residents ​say extreme heat is no longer measured by records but by its impact on daily life, keeping people indoors, reducing social interaction and threatening ‌livelihoods.

The August 2021 record of 48.8 degrees Celsius (119.8 degrees Fahrenheit) turned the Sicilian town into a symbol of Europe’s warming climate as the continent emerged from COVID-19 restrictions.

Today, increasingly frequent and prolonged heatwaves are driving people indoors, leaving streets and piazzas deserted and prompting some residents to compare the extreme heat to a new form of lockdown.

The shift is visible across the town of 20,000 on the outskirts of ​Syracuse, the ancient Greek city on Sicily’s southeastern coast. Piazza del Popolo, long Floridia’s social hub and lined with cafes, palm trees and municipal buildings, is nearly ​empty for much of the day.

The heat lingers well into the evening, disrupting a cherished local tradition known as ’pigghiari u frescu’, when families pull kitchen chairs outside their homes to catch the breeze and socialise.

“It’s awful because many people end up shut indoors. In a way, we are all experiencing another kind ​of lockdown,” Floridia’s culture councillor Serena Spada told Reuters.

“Even people with small children find themselves in this situation. Children cannot go to the park or play outside because, until late ​afternoon, temperatures are genuinely hostile.”

A Warning That Did Not Go Away

On August 11, 2021, Sicily’s Agrometeorological Information Service (SIAS) measured a temperature of 48.8 C in Monasteri, a rural district about 5 km (3 miles) from Floridia’s centre.

In 2024, the World Meteorological Organisation certified it as the highest temperature ever recorded in continental Europe, a mark that still stands.

“As I walked, I began struggling to breathe and thought: ‘I could ​die here in the street, with no one around to help me’,” said resident Ugo Tomasello.

Many residents assumed the record would prove an isolated event. Instead, hot summers became ​the norm.

“It turned out to be a very sad warning sign,” Spada said.

While the temperature record drew international attention, climate scientists say individual extremes are less significant than the steady rise in average ‌temperatures.

Reuters Climate Monitor data showed Florida reached 33.3 C (92 F) on August 12, 2026, 4.1 C (7.4 F) above the average for the 1961-1990 historic norm.

“It is really the increase in average temperatures that worries us,” SIAS director Luigi Pasotti said.

“We are no longer talking about extreme temperature peaks lasting one or two days, as happened in 2021. We are talking about entire weeks, even months during which temperatures remain consistently high.”

Night-time temperatures are climbing too, leaving little respite from the daytime heat.

“This year in particular, we are recording exceptionally high numbers of tropical ​nights in some parts of Sicily, as ​well as super-tropical nights,” Pasotti said.

For Beekeepers, Summer Has Become a Season to Dread

Across Europe, climate change has been linked to increasingly frequent and intense weather extremes, from drought and wildfires to torrential rainfall.

Sicily has emerged as one of Europe’s climate frontlines.

In January, Cyclone Harry produced a record 16.66-metre (55-foot) wave between Sicily ​and Malta. Wildfires have taken a growing toll, with the island accounting for roughly 70 percent of southern Italy’s burned area between January ​and July, according to a Legambiente analysis based on EFFIS-Copernicus data.

Agriculture, a pillar of the island’s economy, is increasingly vulnerable to climate change.

In 2021, more than 3,000 beehives were lost in the area of Floridia and honey production plunged by 80 percent.

“The decline in bee populations and the number of beekeepers, together with the loss of pollinators due to climate change and the widespread use of pesticides, is leading to ​a reduction in biodiversity and lower quality and yields in agricultural production,” agronomist Francesco Bellomi said.

For beekeepers in ​Floridia, summer has become a season of anxiety.

“There’s much more concern about getting through the summer than there used to be,” said beekeeper Francesco Pappalardo, 33, who began working with his father as a child.

“The heat can cause ​individual colonies to collapse and sometimes entire apiaries can be lost, as happened to me in previous years.”

articles.title: Bollywood playback icon Shaan to perform live in Kathmandu on Saturday
articles.summary:
Renowned Indian playback singer Shaan will take the stage at Club Nova tomorrow. The event, ‘Shaan Live in Nepal’, is being brought to the capital by Nepali Touch.

The singer landed in Kathmandu today and will depart on Sunday after his performance. Gates at the venue open at 7 pm, with the show following shortly after.

Shaan will be backed by his own touring band, and audiences can expect a marathon performance. “He will sing more than 40 songs,” said Saugat Regmi, owner of Nepali Touch. “It’s almost a non-stop show; there are no breaks in between, and it will run about two to two-and-a-half hours.”

Describing what Nepali fans can expect from the singer, Regmi said Shaan has a reputation for warmth and stage presence that resonates with local audiences. “He is a generous person, and he’s easily communicative on stage,” he said. “He will open with a Nepali song.”

For the Nepali audience, the concert carries an added layer of nostalgia.

Shaan, known for hits like ‘Chand Sifarish’ (Fanaa), ‘Jab Se Tere Naina’ (Saawariya), ‘Hey Shona’ (Ta Ra Rum Pum), and ‘Suno Na’, who rose to fame in the 1990s, remains one of Bollywood’s most recognisable voices, known for a string of hits across three decades of playback singing.

Shaan Live in Nepal

When: August 22, 2026

Where: Club Nova, Thamel

Time: 7:00 pm onwards

articles.title: Pakistan ex-PM Imran Khan back in jail after shorter-than-expected hospital visit
articles.summary:
A prison van moves past police officers guarding the road leading to Shifa International Hospital after the Supreme Court ordered authorities to move jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan to the hospital, in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 20, 2026.

Pakistan’s former Prime Minister Imran Khan was briefly taken to hospital, ​declared medically fit and sent back to prison within a few hours early on Friday, a surprise move that his supporters and party ‌said violated a top court directive.

The former premier’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party said it would file a contempt petition against what it termed a blatant violation of the Supreme Court order from earlier this week that, according to the party’s interpretation, meant Khan should remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.

Khan said he was being tortured “repeatedly” in prison, his sister, Uzma Khan, who was present during his ​medical examination early on Friday, told reporters at a conference.

There was no immediate response from spokespersons for the interior and law ministries as well as ​from jail authorities to a request for comment from Reuters on Khan’s allegations of torture.

Public perception that the highly popular Khan was moved back to prison forcefully by authorities could spark new outrage among his supporters and potentially escalate tensions and street protests.

‘Contempt of the Judges’

Khan was examined ​at the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, rather than the private Shifa International Hospital mentioned by the court, due to a “security situation created by PTI workers” ​along the planned route, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on X.

The change in venue and the fact that Khan was not given access to his personal physician as mandated by the court, both counted as violation of the court’s order, his party said.

“This is contempt of the judges. This is contempt of the Supreme Court,” Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, ​which is ruled by the PTI, told reporters at the conference, a few hours after Khan had returned to jail.

Khan, who has been in prison since August ​2023, had a patch on one eye, but seemed stable and fit, his sister said.

The cricketer-turned-politician’s supporters lined the streets of the capital Islamabad overnight, showering flowers on the vehicle widely ‌believed to ⁠be carrying him to the hospital.

Aired live on Pakistani television, the images stood in stark contrast to how the country’s broadcasters had covered Khan in recent years, tending to not even cite the ousted leader’s name until Thursday night.

“After what happened yesterday, the pressure (on authorities) will double,” Afridi said, adding that preparations for a protest march planned on September 27 had picked up.

Three Years in Prison

Senior PTI members had expected Khan to remain hospitalized at least for several weeks after he was allowed to leave ​prison to have his health checked for ​the first time since February.

But Pakistan’s Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry told ARY News on Thursday that “if doctors decide that his treatment at the hospital is necessary, he will be admitted. If they opine that he can be treated in jail, he will be sent back.”

“A ​team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist and a physician conducted a detailed examination of him and ​declared him medically fit,” Tarar said on Friday morning.

In its order on Tuesday, the Supreme Court told authorities to transfer Khan to the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and allow him access to a medical panel that includes his personal physician.

Khan was transferred back to Adiala jail in the garrison city of Rawalpindi at 5 am, Tarar said.

Khan has been ⁠imprisoned there since ​2023. He says the cases against him are politically motivated, an accusation the government denies.

His lawyers say ​his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye. The government has said medical reports have disclosed no condition requiring immediate treatment.

articles.title: RSP appoints Pramod Neupane as organisation department chief, Jagdish Kharel as spokesperson
articles.summary:
The Rastriya Swatantra Party has expanded its secretariat and appointed new office-bearers and department chiefs.

A central committee meeting on Friday appointed Pramod Neupane as chief of the organisation department and Jagdish Kharel as the party’s spokesperson.

The meeting appointed Purushottam Yadav as joint general secretary, Manohar Pradhan as treasurer and Basumaya Tamang as joint treasurer. Namita Yadav and Surendra Chaudhary were appointed joint spokespersons.

The party also expanded its secretariat, bringing Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, deputy leader of the parliamentary party Ganesh Parajuli, former general secretary Kabindra Burlakoti, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, Lima Adhikari, Dipakraj Bohara, Sameeksha Baskota, Shiva Nepali, Indira Rana Magar and Manish Jha into the secretariat.

The meeting also nominated Bhupdev Shah, Sudan Gurung, Sunil Lamsal, Pratibha Rawal, Purushottam Yadav, Basumaya Tamang, Surendra Chaudhary, Bhakta Bahadur Rai and Manohar Pradhan as central committee members.

The party also appointed chiefs to several departments. Bijay Jairu will head the public service and public grievances department, Dr Toshima Karki the public health department, Nisha Dangi the infrastructure department, Shisir Khanal the international and diplomacy department, and Lima Adhikari the finance department.

articles.title: A mother came for a citizenship copy. Her son signed it
articles.summary:
For Motikala Oli, getting a replacement copy of her citizenship certificate was a routine government errand. She did not expect it to become a moment she would remember for the rest of her life.

Oli, from Tribeni Rural Municipality-7 in Rukum West, had damaged her original citizenship certificate after it was soaked in water. When she later needed the original document for official business, she had no choice but to apply for a duplicate.

So, early Wednesday morning, she travelled to the District Administration Office in the district headquarters with the documents needed to obtain a replacement.

There was an unexpected twist waiting for her.

The official responsible for issuing the citizenship certificate was her own son, Keshab Prasad Oli, who serves as assistant chief district officer at the office.

As the replacement certificate was being processed, Keshab picked up a red pen and signed his mother’s document.

For him, the moment was as surprising as it was satisfying. His mother’s old certificate had become unusable, and the need for a replacement happened to coincide with his posting as the official authorised to issue citizenship certificates.

“It was damaged after getting wet and could no longer be used,” Keshab said. “We had not really discussed getting a replacement. But on Tuesday afternoon, my mother told me she needed to get her citizenship certificate replaced, so I helped her arrange the documents from the ward office and elsewhere.”

That was when he realised he could be the one to sign it.

“Then I thought, ‘I could actually be the one signing my mother’s citizenship certificate,’” he said. “That made me incredibly happy.”

The moment became even more special when Motikala, carrying the newly prepared replacement certificate, walked into her son’s office for the final signature.

As an official, Keshab had signed hundreds of citizenship certificates during his year-long posting. But this one was different.

Under the section marked “official issuing the duplicate,” he wrote his name and signed the document in red ink. He then handed the certificate to his mother.

He also made sure to capture the moment on camera.

Keshab joined Nepal’s civil service as a section officer in 2018 and has served as assistant chief district officer of Rukum West for the past year. In that time, he has put his signature on hundreds of citizenship certificates.

But signing his mother’s is a moment he considers unique.

“I have signed hundreds of citizenship certificates during the past year, but getting the opportunity to sign my mother’s is a golden moment for me,” he said. “I will remember it for the rest of my life.”

Motikala already knew she would meet her son at the administration office. Keshab had told her that he worked at the chief district officer’s office, so seeing him there was hardly a surprise.

But she did not expect to find him on the other side of the counter, in the very office where citizenship certificates are issued.

Her pride and excitement were unmistakable.

“I was so happy to see that my son had become an official at the CDO’s office. Then he told me, ‘I’ll be the one signing your citizenship certificate.’ I was overjoyed. And in the end, he was the one who handed me the certificate.”

articles.title: Agro Thai Foods to sponsor Nepal Police Club teams for three years
articles.summary:
Agro Thai Foods Pvt. Ltd. has entered into a three-year sponsorship agreement covering the Nepal Police Club’s women’s and men’s volleyball and football teams, as well as its men’s and women’s cricket teams.

The sponsorship agreement was signed on Friday at a programme attended by officials from both sides.

Additional Inspector General Rajan Adhikari, executive director of the National Police Academy and member secretary of the Nepal Police Sports Committee, signed the agreement on behalf of the Nepal Police Physical Fitness and Sports Academy. Sonia Rana, head of the business department at Agro Thai Foods, signed on behalf of the company.

Under the agreement, Agro Thai Foods will provide sponsorship support to the teams for three years.

The sponsorship is expected to strengthen the overall development of the Nepal Police Club’s volleyball, football and cricket teams, while providing greater support for their preparation and participation in competitions.

The partnership is aimed at improving the management, training and preparation of the teams, as well as their branding and participation in national and international tournaments.

Officials at the programme said both parties were committed to fulfilling the terms of the agreement and ensuring that the sponsorship is used to make the teams’ preparations and competition participation more effective and organised.

articles.title: Nepal’s DDC ghee makes its debut in Dubai
articles.summary:
The Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) began its first export of ghee to Dubai on Friday, sending an initial 600 kg shipment under an agreement with Rato ra Chandra-Surya International Pvt. Ltd.

The agreement calls for at least 50,000 kg of ghee to be exported annually. The company is starting with 600 kg to test demand and assess consumer response in the Dubai market.

“We are opening a department store through our subsidiary, Matribhoomi General Trading LLC. The ghee will be sold there,” said Prakash Chandra Ghimire, managing director of Rato ra Chandra-Surya International. “We will place further orders based on the response from the market.”

The shipment marks DDC’s entry into the Dubai market as the company seeks to expand ghee exports beyond its existing destinations and establish a presence in the wider West Asian market.

Ghimire said the ghee has already received a health certificate from the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control based on a laboratory report from DDC. The product will undergo another test in Dubai before it is cleared for sale.

“We have obtained the health certificate from the department based on the DDC’s laboratory report. It is internationally recognised,” Ghimire said. “The product will be tested again in Dubai on that basis.”

The ghee is packed in jars or bottles and has a shelf life of one year, according to the company.

The company plans to expand beyond ghee as well. It is working on exporting yak cheese to Dubai in the future, Ghimire said.

The move into Dubai comes as Nepal continues to export ghee to a small number of overseas markets. According to Department of Customs data, Nepal exported 39,859 kg of ghee worth Rs43.34 million in the last fiscal year.

Japan was by far the biggest market, taking ghee worth Rs43.28 million. Nepal also exported ghee worth Rs51,000 to India, Rs16,000 to the Netherlands and Rs1,000 to the United Kingdom.

“Dubai is a new market for us. This is the first time we are sending ghee there,” Ghimire said.

The company said it plans to use the Dubai market as a stepping stone to expand ghee exports across West Asia.

articles.title: Too many aspirants leave Sudurpaschim chief minister struggling to fill cabinet
articles.summary:
Sudurpaschim Chief Minister Khagaraj Bhatta is struggling to complete his cabinet as more lawmakers from his party, the Nepali Communist Party, seek ministerial posts than there are positions available.

The CPN’s Sudurpaschim provincial committee has recommended 12 lawmakers to the party’s central leadership, which will select three ministers and two ministers of state.

Bhatta was appointed chief minister on August 14 with the support of the CPN-UML. He has already appointed four UML ministers, including one state minister.

With the province limited to seven ministries, including the chief minister’s office, Bhatta can appoint only three more ministers and two state ministers.

“The province has recommended 12 names to the centre because there are more aspirants than available posts,” said Bhanu Bhakta Joshi, the party’s Sudurpaschim in-charge. “The centre will select three ministers and two state ministers from those names and send them to the province.”

Seven of the nominees are from the former CPN (Maoist Centre), three from the former Nagarik Unmukti Party and two from the former CPN (Unified Socialist), all of which merged to form the NCP.

The nominees from the former Maoist Centre are Om Bikram Bhatta, Shiva Singh Oli, Man Bahadur Dhami, Akkal Rawal, Jhapata Saud, Laxmi BK and Janaki Paudel.

From the former Nagarik Unmukti Party, the nominees are Kailash Chaudhary, Khushiram Chaudhary and Indira Giri. Prakash Rawal and Naresh Shahi are from the former Unified Socialist.

articles.title: Ronda Zelezny-Green on how Nepal’s teachers are using AI ‘almost blindly’
articles.summary:
Artificial intelligence is already finding its way into Nepal’s classrooms, even as the education system is still figuring out how to respond to it.

Teachers and students are already using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, according to Ronda Zelezny-Green, an international consultant specialising in AI in education and digital skills and the research lead for the British Council Nepal’s AI4ED project.

The question, she says, is no longer whether AI should be used in education. It is how it can be used to improve learning without creating new problems. “The teachers are ready and open to using generative AI,” Zelezny-Green told The Post. “So now it’s about figuring out how to use it to advance education and learning.”

The first phase of AI4ED involved a national mixed-methods study of 800 teachers. The research found that geography had less influence on AI use than expected. Teachers in urban and rural areas were using AI in broadly similar ways.

Age, however, made a significant difference. Among teachers aged 30 or younger, 94 percent were described as fast AI adopters with experience using AI. Among those aged 50 or older, the figure fell to 54 percent.

Perhaps more striking was what teachers themselves identified as the biggest obstacle.

It was not infrastructure.It was training.

“They don’t know where to get training, and the government isn’t providing it,” Zelezny-Green said. “So they are using AI, but almost blindly.”

The gap could become increasingly important as AI tools become more common in schools. Knowing how to operate an AI chatbot is not the same as knowing how to use it responsibly or effectively.

Zelezny-Green, who has worked on digital skills and education technology across 80 countries, says teachers globally are struggling with the same problem, not just in Nepal. “There simply isn’t enough teacher training,” she said.

For Nepal, that training needs to be designed around the country’s own education system rather than imported wholesale from technology companies. Teachers need to understand not only how to prompt an AI system, but also how to assess its answers, protect sensitive information, and recognise the ethical risks of using such tools.

Data protection is one particular concern. Teachers may not realise that information entered into AI systems can be used for training or other purposes. Responsible AI adoption, therefore, cannot be limited to teachers. Schools, students, and parents all have a role to play. “It needs to be an ecosystem of responsibility shared among everyone who uses AI,” she said.

Nepal also faces another challenge—and an opportunity—in the language gap.

Many of the most widely used AI systems perform far better in English than in Nepali and other local languages. Zelezny-Green says current tools can produce inaccurate translations and culturally unrealistic representations.

But she sees that weakness as an opportunity for Nepal to develop its own solutions.

Smaller language models can be cheaper to develop and maintain than the massive systems behind popular commercial chatbots. Nepal could potentially develop models designed specifically for Nepali and other local languages, using resources already available in the country.

“You have Nepali books here. You have the resources, and the government could support this,” she said. The biggest challenge, she argues, would be access to the computing power needed to train such models—and the political will to make it happen.

That leads to a broader question about who controls the technology, data and infrastructure on which AI depends.

Zelezny-Green argues that Nepal should think seriously about “AI sovereignty”—the idea that countries should not become entirely dependent on foreign companies for AI technologies and infrastructure. “Wholesale reliance on foreign AI technologies, especially expensive American ones, will not be sustainable in the long run,” she said.

But developing local technologies does not solve the question of how AI should be used in classrooms. One of the biggest changes may need to come from the way students are taught and assessed.

For years, education systems have talked about the importance of creativity, collaboration and problem-solving. Generative AI makes those skills even more important because students can now outsource many conventional forms of homework to a chatbot.

Instead of treating this only as a cheating problem, Zelezny-Green argues that schools need to rethink assessment itself. “If a teacher puts in little effort, why should a student work hard when they can simply ask ChatGPT or Claude to do their homework?” she said.

She believes education needs “a new social contract” around AI. That does not mean abandoning foundational skills. In fact, she argues the opposite.

Students first need strong foundations in reading and writing, critical thinking and critical media literacy. They need to be able to recognise misinformation, disinformation and AI-generated content before they can be expected to use AI responsibly.

This is also why she rejects the idea of simply banning AI from schools. “One of my biggest pet peeves is the idea that we should simply ban AI,” she said.

Even students who are not encouraged to use AI will encounter it outside school, she argues. They therefore need to understand what the technology is, what its risks are and how to use it responsibly.For Nepal, that requires policy to catch up with practice.

The country has several policy frameworks dealing with digital development and artificial intelligence. But, according to Zelezny-Green, there is still a gap when it comes specifically to education.

“The biggest gap is training, but there is also a policy gap,” she said. The AI4ED project, she says, could provide evidence for developing such a policy. The challenge is to avoid treating AI as a technological solution to every problem facing Nepal’s education system.

For Zelezny-Green, technology remains secondary to the people using it. “AI in education is a tool, and it will always be a tool,” she said. “It is not a magic wand.”

Technology will continue to change. The more important question, she argues, is whether teachers, students, parents, and policymakers are prepared to lead that change.

Your research found that women’s access to devices and AI does not necessarily close the gender gap. Why is that?

We can’t simply assume that providing devices and internet access will ensure equal participation. One key factor is time poverty. Women and female teachers often have far less time to practice and develop their AI skills because they are also responsible for unpaid care work.

You said AI could help address problems beyond education. What possibilities do you see?

One of the most innovative uses of AI is in addressing climate change, such as predicting floods and other disasters. That is important for education because schools are increasingly affected by climate-related events. AI is also being used to solve long-standing mathematical problems. If it can solve complex maths problems, what about some of these other problems? People need to be more imaginative about what AI can potentially be used for.

You have described AI sovereignty as important for Nepal. What does that mean in practical terms?

Countries do not have to surrender national resources, such as people’s data and data centers, to support AI technologies. Nepal needs to consider what AI sovereignty and independence should look like. Wholesale reliance on foreign AI technologies, especially expensive Western ones, will not be sustainable in the long run.

With all things digital, whether it’s social media or AI, it comes down to how we approach them. So, if you had to roughly weigh the ways people are using AI for harm against the ways they’re using it to improve society, are you more worried or hopeful about where we’re heading?

I’m hopeful because I think there are enough people using AI for good, but there will always be bad actors.

We’re having to think about things we never had to before to stay safe online. One example is voice cloning. For example, having a family passphrase can help verify someone’s identity if their voice has been cloned.

That’s why education has such an important role in the AI era. Almost no one is learning about digital citizenship—what it means to be a responsible citizen in an AI-enabled world. School curricula can help address this, but we’re not really seeing it yet, either globally or in Nepal.

articles.title: ‘What Empire Took, What Empire Left’ confronts the politics of museums, borders, and return in South Asia
articles.summary:
‘What Empire Took, What Empire Left: Museums, Borders and the Politics of Return in South Asia’, an exhibition about the effects in South Asia during Western Occupation, is opening at Taragaon Next, Boudha on August 23. The day will begin with a symposium, followed by the exhibit’s official opening.

Supported by the Saraf Foundation and curated by Arshiya Mansoor Lokhandwala, the exhibit brings together eleven artists from across South Asia and its diaspora to examine how the sacred deities, manuscripts, and ritual objects have been removed from living contexts and reclassified within Western museums. This exhibition confronts that rupture.

The exhibiting artists are Temsüyanger Longkumer, Reetu Sattar, Shaurya Kumar, Raqs Media Collective, Mithu Sen, Divya Mehra, Marium Ghani, LN Tallur, Roshan Mishra, Bishal Manandhar and Jagath Weerasinghe.

“As museums globally confront the colonial histories embedded within their collections, restitution has become one of the defining cultural questions of our time,” says Lokhandwala. “This exhibition brings South Asia into that urgent discourse, asking not simply what should return, but who holds the power to own, interpret and determine the afterlives of displaced heritage.”

‘What Empire Took, What Empire Left’ takes as its starting point a central provocation: what happens when the sacred is violently dislocated—not only from place, but from time, ritual, and meaning?

Spanning Nepal’s emptied temples, the dispersal of India’s bronzes, Gandharan sculpture from Pakistan, and the erosion of Bangladesh’s terracotta heritage, the exhibit traces a region-wide history of cultural dismemberment.

Through contemporary artistic practice, it builds a counter-archive that positions acts of return as a form of epistemic resistance.

What Empire Took, What Empire Left

When: August 23 (Opening)

Where: Taragaon Next, Bauddha

Time: 4:30 pm onwards (Opening)

Entry: Free

articles.title: Dharma Gautam on BP Koirala's enduring legacy
articles.summary:
Dharma Gautam is a writer and political observer who was part of Nepal’s political movement during the Panchayat era, fighting for a multiparty system and advocating for civilians’ rights. He spent time in exile in India, where he began to read extensively and study journalism.

Gautam recently published his first book, ‘BP Ra Bidrohka Ti Din’, which draws on his memories of Nepal’s political struggles and his experiences during exile. The book is prepared from memories and materials he had preserved over the years, following encouragement from friends and family.

The Post’s Shrinkhala Chand Thakuri sat with Gautam to talk about writing, memory, BP Koirala, politics, and books.

How did you get into writing?

Since I was in politics, I wanted to keep up with national and international events and developments. While in college, I regularly listened to foreign radio stations and read any newspapers and magazines I could find.

It was the Panchayat era, so there was no press freedom in Nepal. I regularly read Hindi-language magazines such as ‘Dinman’, ‘Dharmyug’, ‘Kadambini’, ‘Navneet’ and ‘Madhuri’. When these magazines arrived in Ilam, the shopkeepers would first have them censored at the Chief District Officer’s office before putting them up for sale.

After I went into exile in India, I started reading books from different fields. BP himself would give us books and suggest what we should read. Sometimes he would also give us what felt like critical reviews of books he had read.

I also began studying journalism while I was there. BP used to say that newspapers and magazines had a major role in politics.

After returning to Nepal, I began writing about contemporary issues for newspapers. Sometimes a book would affect me, and I would write about it. After the restoration of democracy, I could write openly about political issues. I also wrote about my life in exile and BP’s ideas. Readers seemed to enjoy those pieces, so I continued writing.

I regret not collecting and preserving those writings. Once I began writing regular newspaper columns, I felt compelled to keep writing. I was also requested to contribute pieces for publications, commemorative issues, and memoir collections.

These days, I read and write more slowly because of my age. But I don’t find it difficult to write about subjects I know well. I think my language is also quite simple.

What was it like to revisit the memories you write about in ‘BP Ra Bidrohka Ti Din’?

I prepared this book less out of ambition and more because of pressure from friends and family. Along with that, personally, after last year’s Gen-Z movement, I felt that the new generation should also know the stories of earlier political struggles.

Most of my experiences have already faded from memory. I dived deep into my fading memory and some of the material I had preserved on my computer, then prepared the book with some basic editing.

Reading it made me feel like I was going back in time.

You lived through a very different political Nepal. When you look at young people and politics today, what feels familiar to you?

The struggles are different, but I think there is still an important connection between young people and political change. That is one reason I felt the stories of our generation should be made available to younger people.

You knew BP Koirala personally. What do you remember about him that you don’t often see in accounts of his life?

BP was not only one of the greatest Nepali revolutionaries of our time but also a philosophical thinker.

His socialist thinking was distinctive in the Nepali context. It brought together democracy, individual freedom, social justice, and economic equality. He also had immense compassion for human beings.

He also had a global outlook on politics. Some of his predictions about world events have come true. Whenever I read his books, such as ‘Aatmabrittanta’, I feel that I discover a new meaning in them.

BP also encouraged you to read. How did he influence your reading habits?

BP placed great importance on reading in the development of his personality. He would always complain to us, saying, “You are lazy about reading.”

It doesn’t matter what one reads unless they keep reading. Today, it is not difficult to find material on the subject you are interested in.

You said that you would like to work on BP Koirala’s political thought and philosophy. What aspect of his ideas do you think deserves more attention today?

I would like to work on BP’s political thought and philosophy if I can. His ideas about democracy, individual freedom, social justice, and economic equality remain important.

Five books you think everyone should read?

Reading depends on the individual’s interests, and the choice of books should also be based on that. For someone interested in politics, I think BP Koirala’s writings are essential.

Dharma Gautam’s five book recommendations

Atmabrittanta

Author: BP Koirala

Publisher: Himal Books

It contains BP Koirala’s experiences throughout his life.

Author: Dr Navaraj KC

Publisher: Fineprint Books

‘Swasparsha’ shows how much a doctor can do for society.

Shree 5 ko Sewama

Author: Hemanta Mishra

Publisher: Fineprint Books

The book details Mishra’s experiences working in wildlife conservation.

Letter from Peking

Author: Pearl S Buck

Publisher: John Day Company

This was the first book I read in Grade 8, and it sparked my interest in reading.

Mother Mary Comes to Me

Author: Arundhati Roy

Publisher: Hamish Hamilton

Arundhati Roy’s mother’s fight for her daughter’s right to inherit property is inspiring.

articles.title: Movie review: In ‘Chiso Maanchhe’, a journey with a corpse becomes a meditation on grief and human connection
articles.summary:
There are not many Nepali filmmakers willing to trust their audience to understand their film without announcing its intentions through dialogues. Dipendra K Khanal, however, seems to have given us a space to sit with his images, silences and ambiguities to make sense of ‘Chiso Maanchhe’ on our own.

Released in the theatres in 2022 and on YouTube in 2025, the film begins with a rolling wheel as the radio announces the number of deaths in Nepal during the coronavirus pandemic. Ashok (played by Arpan Thapa) has a mask hanging under his chin and a sanitiser on the edge of his truck’s window.

Ashok, a driver, is hired to take a corpse from Kathmandu to Bajura in his truck. This is a corpse that has freshly arrived from Qatar, one of the major destinations for Nepali migrant workers. Accompanying Ashok are a grieving father, Sher Bahadur (Deshbhakta Khanal), and a widowed wife (Swastima Khadka). The wheels roll and the journey begins.

As they travel from Kathmandu to Bajura, they encounter the broader terror of the widespread virus with the roads engulfed by corpses, migrants, police, and youth patrols. Some go along with them and others obstruct their passage.

With them moving, stopping, negotiating, rebelling and starting again, the story becomes an emblem of the precariousness of life. Along with this, the characters, initially entirely as strangers, begin to understand each other’s worlds, and more importantly, their own.

Khanal, also the director of ‘Aama’, ‘Pashupati Prasad’, ‘Ke Ghar Ke Dera’, is best known for depicting social issues and everyday struggles in his films and he continues doing so in ‘Chiso Maanchhe’. The film shows a broader picture of a frozen, individualistic and isolated society.

In a scene, Khadka’s character is found frolicking in the woods, as though she stumbled upon an oasis. Her father-in-law calls her out, quickly and furiously, and says, “If this was the old days, you would’ve had to become a sati.” The sati is a historical custom where a widow self-immolates on her deceased husband’s funeral pyre.

“If not physically, I have been made a sati in heart,” she says.

It is a line the film never explains, and doesn't need to, because by then, Khanal has already taught us to read what isn't said. Non-verbal cues in the film stand monumental for its provocative ways to communicate its themes and the characters’ emotions.

The truck carrying the corpse of Damber Bahadur, who died of “heart failure” in Qatar, has a quote painted on its back in red. “Life goes on with happiness and laughter. If we work hard, we can find gold in our own country.”

The irony is stark and unmistakable.

Further, these non-verbal cues particularly elaborate the dynamics between Ashok, the driver, and the daughter-in-law.

Whether it’s buying her a bag of titaura to satisfy her cravings or extinguishing his cigarette when she looks uncomfortable, these small, wordless gestures create a sense of intimacy throughout their journey.

With this screenwriting, as commendable as to earn him the ‘Best Writer Award’ for the film, Khanal, however, fails to depict the nuances of his female character. He neither gives a promising background to the daughter-in-law nor a name.

Khadka’s character attempts to run away before retrieving her husband’s dead body. Later, she is found staring at a poster that showed the winner of ‘Nepal Idol’, a singing reality show. We understand consequently that her dream was to become a singer, and that the marriage had not given her enough reasons to grieve her dead husband.

She is given a dream. And a somewhat rebellious nature to chase it. But not enough to earn her a platform of her own.

However, Khadka’s body language, dialect, eye contacts, and even the way she blinks are carefully curated habits to build her character which results in a memorable depiction despite being written unidimensionally.

Ashok, on the other hand, gets to reminisce about his dead wife and six-month-old child whom he left behind with his sister. We understand his financial struggles after he receives a call from his bank warning about the confiscation of his vehicle.

Ashok’s cognitive understanding of self and emotional intelligence add depth to his character.

Costumes of the three lead characters, which are the same throughout the film along with their make-up, also amplify the realism of the film, fitting perfectly into the travel-cinema narrative.

Khanal knew his ways to create a connection between the audience and the screen. With minimal dialogues, the audience, from early on, can get the idea of having to pay close attention to the cinematography, colours, props, and every edge of a frame.

One that stands out the most is the red light inside the truck juxtaposed by the darkness of the outside. Ambience as such gives the film a sense of depth under the warmth, or the discomfort of red.

However, at times, it is almost difficult to put into words the intent of the director. One is compelled to replay some scenes over and over again, simply to understand its underlying motive.

There’s a scene, for instance, where a line of people wearing masks and carrying their belongings walk in a corner of a moving frame. But it is not clear what Khanal is trying to imply with it. After all, why were the people there? Why in a single line? Why were they carrying their belongings and where were they going? Questions like these remain unanswered.

This ambiguity further enters the moral terrain inhabited by the film’s characters. Scenes of dispute and altercation also follow the journey. Yet, every character is given their own motivation and moral ground, resisting the easy division between right and wrong.

Therefore, the film pivots toward a moral question. And Sher Bahadur seems to be the most affected by it. His character, initially a grieving father and a culturally restrictive father-in-law, slowly melts into a man capable of introspection.

‘Chiso Maanchhe’ may seem like it has a slow pace. And it certainly does. But rather than a drawback, it is the film’s conscious choice to demand patience from its viewers.

In the end, the film leaves a corpse, an unrequited love, and a society in transition. It asks us to sit in the cold with its characters. Perhaps the coldness is not only theirs.

articles.title: How Dijup Tuladhar uses AI as part of his everyday toolkit
articles.summary:
Working in US healthcare means I frequently encounter terminology and systems that are unfamiliar in the Nepali context. Previously, understanding a new healthcare concept could require hours or days. Now, I can use AI to break down unfamiliar concepts.

I still verify important information through reliable sources. But AI has shortened the distance.

Building Chordpedia

I founded Chordpedia in 2015 after struggling to find chords for Nepali songs online. The biggest challenge was always execution. AI has changed that equation.

With AI-assisted coding and tools such as ChatGPT, I can move from an idea to a prototype or working feature much faster.

Design and prototyping

Tools such as Figma Make, Lovable and Stitch have changed how I move from an idea to something tangible.

Previously, there was a long process between having an idea and being able to interact with a prototype. Now, I can describe a problem, explore different approaches, generate a prototype, interact with it, identify problems and make changes almost immediately.

However, AI has made the process of designing faster yet hasn't necessarily made deciding what to design easier.

User research and feedback

I use AI to process large amounts of user feedback and identify patterns. It can group similar responses, summarise what users are saying and help him look at competitors from different perspectives.

I look at AI as an assistant. AI can help identify patterns and ask questions, but it cannot always understand the context behind a decision—including users, business priorities, organisational culture and technical limitations.

Everyday life

AI is not limited to my professional life. I also use it for travel planning, learning, comparing options and solving technical problems.

One of my favourite things to do is to use AI to challenge my own thinking.

Instead of asking AI to agree with an idea, I ask it to explain why the idea might be wrong, what I could be missing and what an opposing perspective might look like.

articles.title: An ever-booming Nepali diaspora is being served by severely understaffed missions
articles.summary:
Nepal’s diplomatic missions abroad are struggling with staff shortages as the number of Nepalis living, working and studying overseas continues to rise. This has increased pressure on consular services and limited the missions’ ability to pursue broader diplomatic and economic goals.

The government has repeatedly pledged to strengthen its missions to promote exports, bilateral trade and investment, tourism and economic diplomacy. But missions in countries with rapidly growing Nepali communities say they lack the personnel and resources to deliver even routine services efficiently, let alone pursue those wider objectives.

Japan offers one of the starkest examples.

Nepal opened its embassy in Tokyo in 1965, when roughly 1,000 Nepalis lived in Japan. The mission began with three diplomatic staff. Six decades later, the Nepali community has grown to about 342,000, but the diplomatic establishment has barely changed.

The embassy has five diplomatic positions, including the ambassador. With the ambassadorial post vacant for the past 11 months, only four diplomatic staff are currently working there. Just one position was added last year.

“There were three staff members 61 years ago. Now there are four of us,” Harihar Kant Poudel, chargé d’affaires ad interim, said. “The Nepali diaspora is growing every day, but the resources and staffing of the embassy have not increased accordingly.”

The increase has been particularly rapid in recent years. Japan had about 97,000 Nepalis in 2021, according to the embassy. By August 2026, the number has risen to around 342,000.

The growing population has brought a sharp increase in demand for passports, document verification, powers of attorney and other consular services. The embassy issued about 19,000 passports in the last fiscal year.

Three years ago, applicants would generally receive services on the same day. The embassy now often asks them to leave their documents and return later.

“The workload is so heavy that we are busy even on weekly holidays,” Paudel said.

The pressure is also affecting the embassy’s ability to respond to emergencies. Seventy-three Nepali citizens died in Japan last year for various reasons. The embassy had to assist with the administrative and legal procedures following their deaths, including compensation claims and arrangements concerning their remains, including repatriation. Staff sometimes struggle to visit hospitals and police stations because they are tied up with routine consular work.

The embassy has repeatedly asked the foreign ministry for two additional diplomatic staff and two local employees. It has also sought more resources to assess and verify worker demand, inspect employers, address labour disputes, protect workers’ rights and visit immigration detention centres and prisons to check on Nepali detainees.

Economic diplomacy has suffered. Japan is a major development partner and an important potential source of investment and trade, but embassy officials say they have little time to pursue those opportunities.

Last year, funds allocated by the foreign ministry for economic diplomacy went unused because the mission’s limited staff were occupied with routine consular services.

The embassy in Australia faces similar problems.

Nepal opened its embassy in Canberra in 2007, when only about 7,000 to 8,000 Nepalis lived in Australia. The community now numbers around 300,000. The mission also serves Nepalis in Fiji, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and other countries in the region.

The mission has four diplomatic staff apart from the ambassador, although the ambassadorial position has also been vacant for months.

Tara Gautam, chargé d’affaires ad interim, said hundreds of people visit the embassy for passports, consular services and powers of attorney.

About 150 people come to the embassy each day for passports alone, and staff must process their photographs and biometric data. More than ten applications for powers of attorney, which must be certified by the head of mission, are also received daily.

“I thought the workload would be lighter here than in Saudi Arabia, where I previously worked,” Gautam said. “But it is not. The resources and staff are insufficient for the number of people we serve.”

The embassy has repeatedly requested additional staff.

Foreign Ministry officials acknowledge that most Nepali missions have been operating with bare minimum staff for years.

Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri, spokesperson for the foreign ministry, said the missions were expected to promote Nepal’s interests abroad, economic diplomacy, trade and Nepali culture, while also taking on growing responsibilities for the welfare and protection of Nepalis overseas.

“Our missions are providing maximum services with minimum staff,” he said.

Nepal currently has missions at 45 locations, including embassies in 31 countries, three permanent missions to the UN and other organisations, and ten consulates general, along with a field office in Visakhapatnam, India.

In its budget speech in May, the government announced plans to close the embassies in Denmark, Brazil and South Africa, the consulates general in Chengdu and San Francisco, and the field office in Visakhapatnam. The closures have yet to be completed.

Experts say Nepal’s missions abroad, operating with barely enough staff to function, cannot be expected to deliver on the government’s economic diplomacy ambitions.

Former foreign secretary Madan Kumar Bhattarai says strengthening missions in countries where the Nepali population and economic ties have grown rapidly is essential.

“Where there is greater need and a heavier workload, staffing and other resources should be increased,” he said. “Given the country’s limited financial capacity, priorities should be based on the size of the Nepali diaspora and the economic, commercial, social and cultural importance of each country.”

Staffing levels vary considerably among missions.

The Nepali mission in the United Arab Emirates serves a community of around 700,000 Nepalis. The consulate general in Dubai has only four staff, including the consul general.

Several smaller missions, including those in Myanmar, Brazil, Spain, Denmark and South Africa, have only an ambassador and two diplomatic staff positions. Missions in Ottawa (Canada), Islamabad (Pakistan), Cairo (Egypt), Colombo (Sri Lanka), Tel Aviv (Israel), Paris (France), Berlin (Germany), Brussels (Belgium), Muscat (Oman), Manama (Bahrain), Moscow (Russia), Lisbon (Portugal) and Vienna (Austria) generally have an ambassador and three diplomatic staff. The consulate general in Jeddah (Saudi Arabia) has four staff apart from the consul general.

The embassies in Canberra, Tokyo, Dhaka (Bangladesh), Bangkok (Thailand) and Seoul (South Korea) each have four diplomatic staff positions apart from the ambassador.

Nepal opened its first overseas mission in London in 1934. It currently has five diplomatic staff apart from the ambassador. Nepal’s embassy in Abu Dhabi (UAE) has eight staff, Kuwait seven, Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia) nine, Doha (Qatar) nine, Riyadh (Saudi Arabia) eight and Washington, DC, seven.

Nepal’s permanent mission to the UN in New York has 11 staff, while its permanent missions in Geneva and Vienna have seven and three, respectively. The Nepali consulate general in Kolkata has six staff.

Across all 45 missions, there are currently 244 approved positions, including ambassadors and consul generals. Of these, 47 are held by officials from outside the Foreign Service. They include seven joint secretaries from the civil administration service, seven military attachés, one police counsellor, one intelligence counsellor, nine administrative undersecretaries, two revenue undersecretaries, one legal undersecretary, one accounts undersecretary, nine administrative section officers, three accounts officers, one revenue section officer and five administrative/accounts assistants.

In addition to Foreign Service personnel sent by the ministry, the missions also hire local staff. These include office secretaries, legal advisers, messengers, translators, gardeners, security guards and office assistants, among others.

There are 374 approved positions for local employees. The Foreign Employment Board had been providing financial support for local staff at missions in countries with large numbers of Nepali migrant workers, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Malaysia. The board had been spending Rs25.7 million annually to fund 19 local employees at various embassies. But after the Office of the Auditor General deemed the arrangement contrary to rules, the number of board-funded staff was cut from last year, further increasing the workload on the limited diplomatic staff.

The government has conducted new organisational and management (O&M) surveys for all 17 ministries. Because the surveys were aimed at cutting public expenditure, the Foreign Ministry has been unable to add positions despite its requests for more staff.

The ministry has sought to transfer foreign service staff from the six missions proposed for closure to embassies where additional personnel are needed. However, because the O&M restructuring has not yet been certified by the Prime Minister’s Office, the ministry’s plan has yet to materialise. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Chhetri said the ministry wants to transfer staff from missions proposed for closure to those in need without imposing additional financial burden on the state.

Under the proposal, the ministry would also cut positions in the administration, revenue and accounts groups at missions and replace them with Foreign Service personnel. It has proposed scrapping two minister (economic) positions at the Nepali embassies in New Delhi and Beijing, five consul-general positions in Hong Kong, Lhasa, Kolkata, Chengdu and Guangzhou, and seven joint-secretary-level positions from the administrative service.

It has also proposed cutting labour counsellor positions in the general administration group in Seoul, Kuala Lumpur, Riyadh, Doha and Abu Dhabi, along with the cultural counsellor in New Delhi, the economic counsellor in Visakhapatnam, and nine administrative undersecretary positions, including those from the revenue group in Washington, DC, and Kolkata. The proposal also calls for cutting ten administrative section officer positions at various missions.

Officials from the administrative service have opposed the proposed cuts. Pressure from the administrative service has also meant that Chief Secretary Govinda Bahadur Karki has yet to certify the Foreign Ministry’s O&M proposal.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Hamilton
articles.summary:
Hillcrest functions as the primary campus neighbourhood for Hamilton, operating essentially as the city's main student hub. Rather than a quiet suburban zone, Hillcrest is highly energetic and packed with student flats, local takeaways, and young people walking to lectures. The neighbourhood is completely dominated by university culture, making it the central gathering point for the local international student community.

People can save time and money because they can walk to classes and the university library within minutes, completely eliminating daily bus or parking costs.

Housing demand is incredibly high at the start of semesters, meaning competition for good rooms is fierce, and properties can suffer from student-related noise.

Silverdale serves as a peaceful alternative to the busier streets of Hamilton. It functions as a relaxed retreat where students can study quietly but still reach campus in under five minutes.

Rents are reasonable, and the neighbourhood offers a much calmer, quieter environment that is perfect for focused study.

The area lacks its own major nightlife or dining scene, so people will have to travel to neighbouring suburbs for entertainment or grocery shopping.

Nawton is a well-established residential suburb located on the western side of Hamilton, far from the main university campus. It serves as an excellent hideaway for budget-conscious students who want to escape the university bubble completely.

Weekly rental prices here are among the lowest in the entire city, letting you get a much larger room or property for a lower price.

The commute to the university is long and requires catching a bus through the city centre.

Dinsdale sits elevated on the western hills of Hamilton, acting as a highly independent and fully self-contained suburban community. Rather than just a collection of houses, it features its own comprehensive shopping centres, supermarkets, and medical clinics that cater to all daily needs.

Access to the local amenities means people can buy cheap groceries and essentials right on their doorstep.

Distance from the eastern campus means people are completely dependent on public transport schedules or owning a car to get to their classes.

Hamilton East

Hamilton East is one of the city’s oldest and most character-filled suburbs, blending a trendy heritage vibe with student living. It serves as a creative bridge perfectly positioned right between the university campus and the central business district.

It offers the lifestyle balance in Hamilton, giving students immediate access to food, local employment opportunities, and vibrant weekend river walks.

The charming, older character homes can be poorly insulated, making them quite cold and expensive to heat during the damp winter months.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Hamilton.

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
Two Nepalis were killed after being hit by a train in Romania’s eastern city of Bacău early Sunday morning. Their identities have not yet been disclosed.

According to a statement from the Bacău Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU), the two were struck by a train at around 3:21 am while walking along the railway line near Chimiei Street.

Emergency responders, including ambulances, rescue teams and medical personnel, reached the site shortly after receiving information about the incident. They found both individuals dead upon arrival, the ISU said.

Romanian police and railway authorities have launched an investigation into the accident.

“An investigation is underway to establish how they ended up on the railway line and the circumstances that led to the accident,” the ISU said in its statement.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.
